newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - FX vols off highs as dollar pulls back.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - FX vols off highs as dollar pulls back.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar-pair options were off overnight highs at U.S. midsession as the spot greenback pulled back and time-decay pressure weighed on ahead of the weekend, dealers said.

Still, most traders saw the retreat in both spot and volatilities as a predictable temporary correction to this week's sharp gains and focused on prospects of a sustained high-volatility environment for next week and beyond.
"The anticipated pullback has taken place, but the medium-term trend is still for a higher dollar," Ted Voorhees, a senior trader at Deutsche Bank in New York, said.

The dollar, after piercing the psychologically important 120.00-yen level to a 47-month high overnight, pulled back to around 119.00 yen in U.S. trading. It also tumbled some two pfennigs from a 31-month high of 1.6455 marks touched earlier in the week.

One-month dollar/yen implied volatility was off a quarter point from overnight highs, but up a quarter point on the day, at around 10.4/10.7 percent. One-week dollar/yen was up a full point from Thursday to 11.8/12.8 percent.
One-month dollar/mark lost a quarter point from late Thursday levels to about 9.7/9.9 percent.

A majority of the market was expecting the dollar to either continue testing fresh highs or see sharper retracement in the coming weeks. This was making the market wary of being short gamma and kept the volatility curve inverted in both dollar/mark and dollar/yen.
A short-gamma position, typically achieved by selling shorter-dated options, benefits from time-decay in a quiet market but would be hurt by a large swing in spot rates.
"People don't want to be short gamma because who knows how far it (spot) can pull back, and ultimately it's going to move higher again," Voorhees said.
Kyoko Hiramatsu, a senior dealer at Bank of Yokohama in New York, noted that the market had yet to see full-fledged stop-loss dollar buying, despite the brief poking of the 120-yen barrier.
"Once those stop-losses are touched off, we could see a much higher dollar," she said. "So it's just not a situation to sell short-dated options."

She added that, taking a step back, the dollar had risen so quickly to multi-year highs that many people did not have a lot of options with higher strike prices and needed to restructure their positions.

Due in part to such broad demand, risk reversals, which reflect pricing differential between out-of-the-money puts and calls, stayed skewed for yen puts. Traders said it was the first time in several years that they had favored yen puts for more than a few days.
One-month 25-delta dollar/yen stood at 0.2/0.5 percent bid for yen puts, little changed from Thursday.

Elsewhere, Swiss franc and sterling volatilities were firm because of turbulent trading lately in their respective spot markets. One-month dollar/Swiss rose a quarter point to 11.9/12.2 percent, while cable was steady at 9.8/10.2 percent.
